facts.text: Peter S. Beagle's 1968 novel, which he adapted into this screenplay, has sold more than six million copies and been translated into at least 25 languages.
The songs by Jimmy Webb, performed by the band America, were written before any animation was drawn, so the animators worked to the music like old Disney shorts.
Voices were recorded first in New York under co-director Jules Bass. Tokyo animators then drew to the tracks with lip-sync charts, even though they didn't fully understand the English dialogue.
Variety's Todd McCarthy panned the animation but wrote that Mia Farrow's voice gives the Unicorn a plaintive quality, calling it a rare feat for an actress to register so strongly on voice alone.
The film's look came from Lester Abrams' early sketches and Topcraft artist Tsuguyuki Kubo, who co-designed the characters and co-storyboarded. His concept work dates to November 1979.
The butterfly quotes Elvis, the Andrews Sisters and Duke Ellington's 'Take the A Train', centuries before any of them existed. In a movie set in Robin Hood's era, that's quite the anachronism.
Producer Michael Chase Walker bought the film rights outright about two weeks before his option ran out, a purchase worth roughly $200,000 in today's money.
Topcraft's Tokyo animators drew about 75,000 drawings and used around 260 colors. Typical Japanese animation of the day used 80 to 130.
Peanuts TV-special producers Lee Mendelson and Bill Melendez once wanted to adapt the novel. Beagle says a partner's wife warned him they weren't good enough, and the project died.
Angela Lansbury, voicing the witch Mommy Fortuna, was making her first voice performance in a theatrical film. She later voiced Mrs. Potts in Beauty and the Beast (1991).
Mommy Fortuna is named for Fortuna, the Roman goddess of luck, who brought both good and bad fortune to humans.
Producer Michael Chase Walker hoped for a $5 million budget. The finished film reportedly cost closer to $3.5 million, possibly less, and it still never turned a profit.
The name of Alan Arkin's character, the bumbling magician Schmendrick, comes from the Yiddish word 'schlemiel', meaning an unlucky bungler.
The harpy is named Celaeno, a real figure from Greek and Roman myth. The name means 'the dark one', and Virgil's Aeneid is the oldest surviving source for it.
Beagle was furious that Rankin/Bass got the job. He reportedly yelled at producer Michael Chase Walker, who answered that Hanna-Barbera were next on the list.
Beagle wrote the script for Ralph Bakshi's 1978 The Lord of the Rings, and Rankin/Bass made TV versions of The Hobbit and The Return of the King. This film is full of Middle-earth connections.
Early press billed the film as an 'adult musical fantasy-adventure', and Rankin/Bass cast actors like Alan Arkin, Mia Farrow and Christopher Lee to appeal to grown-ups, not just kids.
Even Beagle had a note about the voices. He said Alan Arkin's Schmendrick seemed 'too flat' to him, though he praised nearly everyone else in the cast.
Alan Arkin was a founding member of the folk group The Tarriers and co-wrote 'The Banana Boat Song' ('Day-O'), which became a huge hit for Harry Belafonte.
The riddle 'Why is a raven like a writing desk?' is the Mad Hatter's unanswerable riddle from Alice in Wonderland. Lewis Carroll wrote it with no answer at all.
Unusually for an animated film, stars including Mia Farrow, Alan Arkin, Angela Lansbury and Tammy Grimes recorded their lines together over two or three days.
Topcraft reportedly spent 2 million yen on an artbook so its artists could study the fairy-tale illustrator Kay Nielsen, whose work influenced the film's forest backgrounds.
Keenan Wynn voices both the bandit Captain Cully and the harpy Celaeno. Paul Frees does triple duty too, as the wizard Mabruk, the Cat and the amorous Tree.
In 1978 Warner Bros. reportedly paid producer Michael Chase Walker $25,000 a month in a development deal for this film. When Warner dropped it, the money became debt he owed the studio.
Dustin Hoffman, Harrison Ford and Mark Hamill were all considered for the voice of Schmendrick before Alan Arkin got it.
According to Mental Floss, Rankin/Bass never had to settle for a second choice: every actor they approached for a voice role said yes right away.
The love-struck tree is voiced by Paul Frees. Actors Don Messick and Nellie Bellflower were credited for years, but the Blu-ray's making-of confirmed those credits were wrong.
Molly Grue's swearing at the Unicorn ('Damn you!') was cut or dubbed over in the 2007 25th Anniversary DVD, even though the film is nominally G-rated.
Tammy Grimes (Molly Grue) was offered the lead role of Samantha on Bewitched but turned it down for the stage. Elizabeth Montgomery got the part.
Universal was set to distribute but reportedly wasn't enthusiastic. The film ended up with a small Utah distributor, and director Arthur Rankin Jr. said the box office was 'not too good'.
Imagine magazine's Colin Greenland singled out the Red Bull, a creature made entirely of fire, as one of the film's best-realized bursts of imagination.
Listen closely to the dragon's roars later in the film. They reportedly reuse the roars from the old Japanese Godzilla movies.
The New York Times' Janet Maslin called it 'an unusual children's film in many respects, the chief one being that it is unusually good.'
facts.byline: Janet Maslin — The New York Times

facts.text: Sir Christopher Lee (King Haggard) arrived at recording sessions with his own copy of the novel, marked with passages he insisted must not be cut.
Jeff Bridges (Prince Lir) phoned director Jules Bass out of the blue, offering to do the film for free because the novel was a favorite. He also recommended songwriter Jimmy Webb.
King Haggard was almost voiced by James Earl Jones, John Vernon or John Carradine. Sir Christopher Lee got the role.
The soundtrack album came out in Germany on Virgin Records in 1983, not in the US, and was one of West Germany's best-selling albums of that year.
The band America's Dewey Bunnell says they often play the film's title song on German tours, because audiences there love it. The film was a huge hit in Germany.
Topcraft photographed a clay model of King Haggard's castle under colored lights and used the photos as reference. Some effects were made by shining colored light through holes cut in the artwork.
Mia Farrow's singing in 'Now That I'm a Woman' was dubbed by studio singer Katie Irving. The song is missing from the film's original theatrical and HBO versions.
The Cat's gag of flipping over his eye-patch to show he doesn't need it wasn't in the script. One of the Japanese animators improvised it.
In the novel the Skull is only a skull. The Japanese animators gave it a body, and Orson Welles was once considered to voice it.
Art Garfunkel covered 'That's All I've Got to Say', the Jimmy Webb song sung by Jeff Bridges' Prince Lir, to close his album Scissors Cut.
Singer Fergie loved the film as a kid. In 2015 Playbill reported she planned a stage musical of it with then-husband Josh Duhamel, but it never got off the ground.
While Sir Christopher Lee recorded King Haggard's speech about unicorns bringing him joy, author Peter S. Beagle visited. Lee begged for his approval and offered to redo the take.
In 2003 the Online Film Critics Society ranked The Last Unicorn the 96th greatest animated film of all time, a long way up for a movie that flopped on release.
The VHS/DVD cut extends the Skull's scene, including Schmendrick's quip 'Walk through a clock? What do I look like, a magician?' The theatrical version is shorter.
Distributor Jensen Farley opened the film on November 19, 1982 and soon went bankrupt. Rankin/Bass and the other producers never saw a profit.
Topcraft, the Tokyo studio that animated this film, was hired by Hayao Miyazaki for Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind. Its core staff later formed Studio Ghibli.
A US flop, but a hit in Germany, where it reportedly out-grossed Star Wars. Huge 'The Unicorn is Coming!' posters went up on buildings in Munich.
Beagle didn't know how to feel about the film for years. After many viewings he realized he thought it was a classic.
Beagle refused to write a sequel for decades. In 2005 he wrote the short story 'Two Hearts', set after the film's events with Schmendrick, Molly and Lir, who is now a king.
A live-action remake has been in development hell for years, with Christopher Lee and Angela Lansbury once attached to return. Legal disputes and budget issues stalled it.
It opened in 648 US theaters on November 19, 1982, and made $2.25 million its first weekend. It finished with about $6.5 million in the US and Canada.
A scene from the novel with a princess begging Prince Lir for help was designed and animated, but cut from the final film.
Dan Avidan of Game Grumps and Ninja Sex Party released a cover of the theme song in 2015, bringing a new audience to the film.
